title: Mars Outpost: Astronaut Challenges
ratingNote: Ratings are preliminary assessment-design ratings, not official NASA judgements.
scienceNote: These are simplified educational scenarios, not operational instructions for real astronauts. Actual mission decisions require authorised procedures, engineering data and expert judgement.

questions.title: Oxygen Alarm
questions.scenario: You are inside the Mars habitat when the oxygen alarm sounds. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the crew, check the warning and follow the emergency oxygen procedure.
Ignore the alarm and continue your work.
Open the habitat door to let Mars air inside.

questions.title: Low Battery
questions.scenario: The habitat battery is running low. What should your crew do?

options.text: Switch off lights and equipment that are not needed.
Turn on every light and machine.
Use the remaining power for entertainment.

questions.title: Saving Water
questions.scenario: The water supply is getting low. What is the best action?

options.text: Use water carefully and check the recycling system.
Leave taps running.
Use drinking water to wash the rover.

questions.title: Cold Greenhouse
questions.scenario: The plants in your Mars greenhouse are getting too cold. What should you do?

options.text: Check the heating system and protect the plants.
Turn off all heating.
Move the plants outside the habitat.

questions.title: Dusty Air Filter
questions.scenario: Mars dust is blocking the habitat air filter. What should the crew do?

options.text: Clean or replace the filter using the correct safety procedure.
Add more dust to the filter.
Ignore the air-quality warning.

questions.title: Dusty Solar Panels
questions.scenario: Dust has covered the solar panels and less electricity is being produced. What should you do?

options.text: Arrange a safe inspection and cleaning of the panels.
Paint the panels black.
Keep using more electricity without checking them.

questions.title: Food Supplies
questions.scenario: Some stored food may spoil soon. What should the crew do?

options.text: Check the food and use safe items that need to be eaten first.
Throw away all the food immediately.
Hide the food and stop checking supplies.

questions.title: Weak Radio Signal
questions.scenario: The radio antenna is not sending a clear signal to Earth. What should you do?

options.text: Check the antenna and use the backup communication system if needed.
Damage the antenna further.
Stop all communication attempts.

questions.title: Oxygen Tank Leak
questions.scenario: A sensor reports that oxygen is leaking from a storage tank. What should happen?

options.text: Tell the crew and isolate or repair the leak according to the safety plan.
Ignore the warning.
Open the tank and let more oxygen escape.

questions.title: Mars Rock Study
questions.scenario: Your rover finds an unusual rock near the habitat. What is the best next step?

options.text: Use the rover to photograph and study it safely.
Drive the rover into an unsafe area to reach it quickly.
Ignore the rover's safety instructions.

questions.title: Dust Storm Warning
questions.scenario: A large dust storm is approaching your Mars base. What should the crew do?

options.text: Secure equipment, remain in the habitat and conserve power.
Go outside to watch the storm.
Leave doors and equipment exposed.

questions.title: Solar Radiation Alert
questions.scenario: Mission control reports a possible solar radiation event. What should astronauts do?

options.text: Follow the radiation safety plan and move to the designated protected area if instructed.
Go outside to watch the Sun.
Ignore the alert.

questions.title: Very Cold Conditions
questions.scenario: The outside temperature is becoming extremely cold. What should you protect?

options.text: Habitat heating, life-support equipment and temperature-sensitive systems.
Outdoor furniture first.
Nothing; all equipment works at any temperature.

questions.title: Rover Stuck
questions.scenario: Your exploration rover becomes stuck in soft ground. What should the crew do?

options.text: Stop unsafe movement and plan a careful recovery.
Keep driving faster into the soft ground.
Leave it running until its battery is empty.

questions.title: Possible Water Ice
questions.scenario: A rover detects a material that may be water ice. What should you do?

options.text: Investigate and test a sample using approved equipment.
Assume it is safe drinking water immediately.
Damage the area before recording it.

questions.title: Unhealthy Plants
questions.scenario: Some greenhouse plants show signs of disease. What should the crew do?

options.text: Separate affected plants and inspect them carefully.
Mix all plants together.
Stop caring for every plant.

questions.title: Habitat Pressure Warning
questions.scenario: The habitat pressure is falling. What is the safest response?

options.text: Check for a leak and follow the habitat emergency procedure.
Open a hatch to the outside.
Ignore the pressure sensor.

questions.title: Dusty Greenhouse Window
questions.scenario: Dust is blocking sunlight from reaching the greenhouse. What can help?

options.text: Clean the window safely or use suitable plant lights.
Cover the window with more dust.
Stop monitoring the plants.

questions.title: Rover Navigation Problem
questions.scenario: Your rover is unsure of its location. What should it do?

options.text: Stop in a safe place and check its map and navigation sensors.
Drive as fast as possible.
Switch off all navigation sensors.

questions.title: Astronaut Feels Unwell
questions.scenario: A crew member says they are feeling unwell. What should you do?

options.text: Inform the crew medical officer and follow the medical plan.
Tell them to ignore it.
Send them outside alone.

questions.title: Overheating Battery
questions.scenario: The battery system is getting too hot. What should the crew do?

options.text: Check the system and use its approved cooling procedure.
Cover it with a blanket.
Continue charging without monitoring it.

questions.title: Crack in the Habitat
questions.scenario: You notice a crack or possible damage on the habitat wall. What should happen?

options.text: Report it, keep away from the damaged area and arrange an inspection and repair.
Make the crack larger.
Hide the damage.

questions.title: Oxygen Machine Stops
questions.scenario: The machine that produces oxygen has stopped. What should the crew do?

options.text: Use the backup life-support procedure and arrange a repair.
Turn off the oxygen alarm.
Wait until all stored oxygen is gone.

questions.title: Robot Needs Repair
questions.scenario: A maintenance robot stops working. What should the crew do?

options.text: Check the fault and repair it safely or use another approved method.
Hit it until it starts.
Send it on another mission while it is damaged.

questions.title: Ice-Drilling Machine Fails
questions.scenario: The machine used to investigate underground ice stops working. What should you do?

options.text: Make the equipment safe, inspect the fault and arrange a repair.
Use all drinking water to test it.
Ignore the failure.

questions.title: Waiting for Earth
questions.scenario: You have sent a question to Earth, but the reply will take time. What should the crew do?

options.text: Use the approved onboard procedures while waiting for guidance.
Make a dangerous guess.
Stop monitoring the habitat.

questions.title: Not Enough Repair Materials
questions.scenario: Your team needs materials to repair part of the base. What is a sensible action?

options.text: Check approved spare parts and safe reusable materials.
Use unknown materials without testing them.
Throw away all useful equipment.

questions.title: Leaking Water Pipe
questions.scenario: A pipe in the greenhouse is leaking water. What should happen?

options.text: Stop the leak and protect the remaining water supply.
Let the water continue to escape.
Open more water pipes.

questions.title: Science Equipment Needs Power
questions.scenario: A science instrument needs electricity, but life-support equipment also needs power. What should the crew do?

options.text: Keep essential life-support systems supplied before using spare power for science.
Give all power to the science instrument.
Switch off oxygen production.

questions.title: Backup Generator Failure
questions.scenario: The backup generator stops working. What should the crew do?

options.text: Conserve power and arrange a safe inspection and repair.
Use more electricity than usual.
Ignore the failure.

questions.title: Major Solar Storm
questions.scenario: A strong solar storm warning reaches your Mars outpost. What should the crew do?

options.text: Follow the shelter procedure and pause non-essential outdoor activities.
Go outside to take photographs.
Continue outdoor work without checking the warning.

questions.title: Very Low Oxygen
questions.scenario: The stored oxygen level is becoming dangerously low. What should happen first?

options.text: Protect the crew and follow the emergency life-support procedure.
Use oxygen for a non-essential experiment.
Ignore the oxygen reading.

questions.title: Two Systems Fail
questions.scenario: The oxygen system and the radio both stop working. Which issue should receive immediate priority?

options.text: Protect the crew's oxygen supply while using emergency communication procedures.
Focus only on the radio and ignore oxygen.
Do not respond to either failure.

questions.title: External Repair
questions.scenario: An astronaut may need to leave the habitat to repair equipment. What must be checked first?

options.text: Suit condition, task risks, environmental conditions and the approved EVA plan.
Go outside without a spacesuit.
Rush outside without checking equipment.

questions.title: Food Supply Shortage
questions.scenario: The food supply is lower than expected. What should the crew do?

options.text: Check remaining supplies, plan meals carefully and use approved emergency provisions.
Eat all remaining food immediately.
Stop checking the greenhouse.

questions.title: Smoke Alarm
questions.scenario: A smoke alarm activates inside the habitat. What should the crew do?

options.text: Follow the fire response procedure and protect the crew.
Cover the alarm and continue working.
Keep operating equipment that may be overheating.

questions.title: Rover Stops Communicating
questions.scenario: An exploration rover stops sending information. What should the team do?

options.text: Try the approved recovery and communication procedure before sending help.
Assume it is safe and forget about it.
Send every available rover away at once.

questions.title: Water and Oxygen Power Demand
questions.scenario: The water-recycling and oxygen systems both need more electricity. What should guide the decision?

options.text: Protect essential crew needs and manage the available power carefully.
Use power for decorations first.
Switch off both systems.

questions.title: Improve the Storm Shelter
questions.scenario: The crew can improve the shelter used during radiation warnings. What is the best approach?

options.text: Use suitable shielding materials and keep essential supplies accessible.
Remove the shelter walls.
Use the shielding materials for unrelated tasks.

questions.title: Conflicting Messages
questions.scenario: Two messages from Earth appear to give different instructions. What should the crew do?

options.text: Check message details and follow the authorised mission and safety procedures.
Choose one randomly.
Ignore all instructions and safety rules.

questions.title: Explore a Possible Ice Deposit
questions.scenario: A rover finds a location that may contain underground ice. What should your team do next?

options.text: Plan a careful investigation using the rover's instruments.
Start drilling without checking the ground or equipment.
Use all habitat power immediately.

questions.title: Long Rover Journey
questions.scenario: A rover is travelling far from the habitat. What should be checked before departure?

options.text: Battery, route, communication, terrain and a safe return plan.
Only the rover's colour.
Nothing; the rover can manage every situation.

questions.title: Expand the Greenhouse
questions.scenario: The crew wants to grow more food. What should be planned first?

options.text: Available water, power, space, equipment and expected food needs.
Build immediately without checking resources.
Use all drinking water for plants.

questions.title: Prepare for Low Solar Power
questions.scenario: Forecasts suggest that solar panels may produce less electricity over the next few days. What should you do?

options.text: Conserve energy and reserve power for essential systems.
Use all stored battery power today.
Leave every machine running.

questions.title: Damaged Antenna
questions.scenario: A dust storm damages the main antenna. What should the crew do?

options.text: Use backup communication and plan a safe antenna repair.
Throw away all communication equipment.
Stop following mission procedures.

questions.title: Unusual Mars Rock
questions.scenario: A rover finds an unusual rock formation. What is a useful scientific response?

options.text: Record images and collect a sample if the mission plan permits.
Damage the rover to reach it.
Collect samples without recording their locations.

questions.title: Medical Supplies Running Low
questions.scenario: The medical supplies are running low. What should the crew do?

options.text: Check the inventory, protect essential supplies and request resupply if available.
Use medical supplies for non-medical tasks.
Hide the shortage from the crew.

questions.title: Build Another Habitat Room
questions.scenario: The team proposes building another room. What should be assessed?

options.text: Construction materials, power, safety, time and crew requirements.
Only the room's appearance.
Start construction without a plan.

questions.title: Strengthen the Radiation Shelter
questions.scenario: The crew wants to improve its radiation shelter. What should be considered?

options.text: Suitable shielding design, materials, access and essential supplies.
Remove the shelter roof.
Store all supplies outside the habitat.

questions.title: Extend the Mission
questions.scenario: Mission control asks whether the crew can remain on Mars longer. What must be reviewed?

options.text: Food, water, oxygen, power, equipment condition and crew health.
Only the number of experiments completed.
Agree without checking any supplies.

questions.title: Severe Solar Event
questions.scenario: A severe solar event is forecast. What should the crew do?

options.text: Move to the designated protected area and follow radiation procedures.
Go outside to observe it.
Ignore the warning.

questions.title: Solar Power System Failure
questions.scenario: The solar panels stop supplying electricity. What should happen?

options.text: Conserve battery power and arrange a safe inspection and repair.
Switch on every machine.
Use all backup power for non-essential tasks.

questions.title: Two Habitat Leaks
questions.scenario: Two habitat sections may be losing air. What should the crew do?

options.text: Protect the crew, isolate affected areas as required and follow repair procedures.
Open both sections to inspect them without protection.
Ignore the pressure alarms.

questions.title: Food and Water Shortage
questions.scenario: Food and water supplies are both low. What is the best response?

options.text: Protect essential crew needs, use reserves carefully and reduce waste.
Use all supplies immediately.
Waste water on non-essential cleaning.

questions.title: Rescue a Stranded Rover
questions.scenario: A rover carrying valuable samples becomes stuck. What should guide the rescue decision?

options.text: Keep the crew and habitat safe while assessing the risks and resources needed.
Risk the habitat's essential power to recover every sample.
Send another rover without checking its battery.

questions.title: Limited Power for Essential Systems
questions.scenario: The habitat has very little electricity. Which systems should receive priority?

options.text: Oxygen, water, thermal control and other essential life-support systems.
Decorative lights and entertainment equipment.
Only the science display.

questions.title: Meteorite Impact
questions.scenario: A small meteorite strikes an external part of the habitat. What should the crew do?

options.text: Check for damage and keep people away from unsafe areas until inspected.
Ignore the impact.
Touch damaged electrical equipment.

questions.title: No Contact with Earth
questions.scenario: The habitat loses communication with Earth. What should the crew do?

options.text: Use the onboard emergency plan and attempt backup communication.
Stop all safety checks.
Make an unplanned risky decision.

questions.title: Final Science Opportunity
questions.scenario: A rare science opportunity appears, but the habitat has limited power. What should the crew do?

options.text: Confirm essential systems have sufficient power before approving the experiment.
Use all power for the experiment.
Switch off oxygen production.

questions.title: End-of-Mission Review
questions.scenario: Your crew has completed its planned stay on Mars. What should be checked before the next mission phase?

options.text: Crew health, habitat safety, supplies, equipment condition and mission records.
Only the number of experiments completed.
Leave without checking the habitat.

questions.title: Life-Support Power Priority
questions.scenario: A Mars habitat has limited electrical power. Oxygen production, laboratory instruments and non-essential lighting are operating. What should the commander prioritise?

options.text: Maintain essential life-support systems and reduce non-essential electrical loads.
Keep every system at maximum power.
Prioritise laboratory instruments regardless of oxygen reserves.

questions.title: Battery Reserve Planning
questions.scenario: A dust storm is forecast to reduce solar generation for two days. The battery is at 70%. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Reduce non-essential loads and protect a reserve for critical systems.
Continue normal consumption and wait until the battery is nearly empty.
Increase experimental activity before the storm.

questions.title: Water-Recovery Fault
questions.scenario: The water-recovery system is operating at half capacity. Which response best protects the mission?

options.text: Diagnose and repair the fault while monitoring reserves and limiting avoidable water use.
Use stored water without changing operations.
Stop measuring water consumption until repairs are complete.

questions.title: Greenhouse Energy Trade-off
questions.scenario: The greenhouse requires additional lighting while habitat battery reserves are low. What is the most balanced response?

options.text: Schedule or reduce lighting while preserving required power for life support.
Allocate all available power to the greenhouse.
Disable plant lighting indefinitely without assessing crop requirements.

questions.title: Air-Quality Warning
questions.scenario: A sensor indicates declining habitat air quality. What should the crew do first?

options.text: Verify the measurement, inspect filtration and follow the relevant safety procedure.
Disable the sensor because it may be faulty.
Open the habitat to the external Martian atmosphere.

questions.title: Solar-Array Dust Accumulation
questions.scenario: Solar-array output has decreased after a dust event. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Assess array performance and arrange a safe cleaning or maintenance procedure if needed.
Assume output will recover immediately without inspection.
Increase electrical demand to compensate for lower generation.

questions.title: Food Inventory Planning
questions.scenario: Stored food will last 18 days, but the mission must continue for 25 days. What should the crew do?

options.text: Recalculate consumption, assess crop production and activate a contingency supply plan.
Continue current consumption and assume extra food will appear.
Stop recording food inventory.

questions.title: Communication Outage
questions.scenario: The primary antenna fails during a routine operation. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Use the backup communication plan and continue only within approved mission procedures.
Attempt a high-risk operation because Earth cannot respond.
Disable onboard monitoring systems.

questions.title: Habitat Pressure Loss
questions.scenario: Habitat pressure begins to decrease slowly. What should the crew do?

options.text: Locate the source, isolate affected sections if necessary and protect the crew.
Wait until pressure reaches a critical level before acting.
Open another hatch to equalise pressure with the outside.

questions.title: Science Versus Survival
questions.scenario: A high-value experiment requires power also needed by life-support equipment. Which decision principle is soundest?

options.text: Protect critical crew-safety systems before allocating surplus power to science.
Always choose the experiment because of its research value.
Split power equally even if life support becomes inadequate.

questions.title: Solar Particle Event Alert
questions.scenario: A space-weather alert indicates an elevated solar particle event risk. What should the mission team do?

options.text: Review the event context and follow radiation-monitoring and shelter procedures, limiting unnecessary EVA.
Continue all outdoor activities without reviewing the alert.
Assume the alert means the surface is immediately unsafe or immediately safe without checking details.

questions.title: Radiation Shelter Readiness
questions.scenario: A habitat has a designated storm shelter with additional shielding. What should determine crew movement during a serious solar radiation warning?

options.text: The mission's radiation procedures and verified warning information.
The shelter's distance from the largest window.
A preference to remain near external equipment.

questions.title: Dust-Storm Operations
questions.scenario: A regional dust storm reduces visibility and solar generation. Which operational response is strongest?

options.text: Pause exposed activities, secure equipment and shift to essential power loads.
Schedule additional rover trips during peak storm conditions.
Ignore power forecasts because batteries are unlimited.

questions.title: Thermal-Control Failure
questions.scenario: A habitat cooling loop is failing and equipment temperature is rising. What is the best response?

options.text: Protect crew-critical thermal control, isolate the fault and reduce non-essential heat loads.
Keep all equipment operating at maximum output.
Disable temperature sensors to remove alarms.

questions.title: EVA Timing Decision
questions.scenario: An astronaut must perform an external repair while radiation and dust conditions are uncertain. What should determine whether the EVA proceeds?

options.text: Verified environmental data, suit readiness, task urgency and mission safety limits.
The desire to complete the task as quickly as possible.
A fixed schedule regardless of current conditions.

questions.title: Dust on Optical Sensors
questions.scenario: A rover's cameras and navigation sensors become obscured by dust. What is the best action?

options.text: Check sensor status, use approved cleaning or backup navigation methods and reassess the route.
Continue at full speed using unreliable images.
Disable obstacle detection.

questions.title: Cold-Soak Risk
questions.scenario: An external instrument may become too cold during a long night. What should planners do?

options.text: Use its thermal limits and power budget to schedule operation or a safe shutdown.
Assume the instrument works at any temperature.
Leave it powered without monitoring.

questions.title: Solar-Power Forecast
questions.scenario: Forecasts indicate several low-generation days ahead. Which plan best reduces risk?

options.text: Estimate demand, conserve energy and maintain reserves for essential loads.
Spend the reserve before the low-generation period begins.
Avoid planning because forecasts contain uncertainty.

questions.title: Radiation Data Interpretation
questions.scenario: A dashboard shows a radiation alert but provides no units, timestamp or source. What should the operator do?

options.text: Check the original data, units, timestamp and measurement context before interpreting the value.
Treat the number as a confirmed astronaut dose.
Compare it directly with an unrelated game percentage.

questions.title: Environmental Sensor Disagreement
questions.scenario: Two sensors report different temperatures near an external instrument. What is the best approach?

options.text: Check calibration, location and sensor health, then use validated measurements.
Choose whichever reading is more convenient.
Average the values without checking whether they measure the same thing.

questions.title: Battery Degradation
questions.scenario: Battery capacity has declined over repeated charge cycles. What should mission planners do?

options.text: Update usable-capacity estimates and revise the energy budget with an appropriate reserve.
Continue using the original capacity rating.
Increase loads to test the battery during an emergency.

questions.title: Redundant Oxygen Production
questions.scenario: The primary oxygen-generation unit is unreliable. Why is a suitable backup capability valuable?

options.text: It provides an alternate capability if the primary unit fails, subject to backup limits.
It guarantees oxygen can never run out.
It removes the need to monitor the primary unit.

questions.title: Life-Support Maintenance Window
questions.scenario: A filter requires scheduled maintenance, but the crew is busy with science activities. What is the best decision?

options.text: Schedule maintenance before performance becomes unsafe, following approved procedures.
Delay all maintenance until a failure occurs.
Remove the filter while the system continues operating normally.

questions.title: Habitat Leak Isolation
questions.scenario: A leak is detected in one module connected to the main habitat. What is the main benefit of isolating that module?

options.text: It can limit atmosphere loss and protect the remaining habitable volume.
It automatically increases oxygen throughout the habitat.
It repairs the leak without inspection.

questions.title: Local Material for Shielding
questions.scenario: A rover identifies material that may be useful for radiation shielding. What should happen before it is used in construction?

options.text: Characterise its properties and verify suitability for the intended engineering use.
Assume all local materials provide equal protection.
Use it immediately without testing.

questions.title: Repair or Replace
questions.scenario: A pump is failing intermittently. Which information best supports a repair-versus-replacement decision?

options.text: Failure history, diagnosis, spare availability, repair time and mission risk.
The pump's colour alone.
Which option uses fewer words in the maintenance log.

questions.title: Rover Energy Budget
questions.scenario: A rover must travel to a site, conduct measurements and return to base. What should its energy plan include?

options.text: Outbound travel, terrain, science operations, communications and a return reserve.
Only the energy required to reach the destination.
The advertised maximum battery capacity with no margin.

questions.title: Thermal and Power Trade-off
questions.scenario: Heaters consume electricity also needed by other systems. What is the best design approach?

options.text: Improve insulation and schedule heating while maintaining required temperature limits.
Turn off all heating regardless of temperature.
Use maximum heating continuously without measuring demand.

questions.title: Critical-System Redundancy
questions.scenario: Why should critical systems have independent backup capability where feasible?

options.text: A single failure is less likely to endanger the mission if a suitable backup is available.
Backups make testing and maintenance unnecessary.
A backup system always has unlimited capacity.

questions.title: Fault Diagnosis
questions.scenario: A machine stops unexpectedly. What should the crew do before attempting a repair?

options.text: Make the system safe, review alarms and diagnose the likely fault using procedures.
Disconnect random components immediately.
Restart repeatedly without checking for damage.

questions.title: Communication Delay
questions.scenario: A command from Earth cannot arrive before a time-critical decision. What capability is essential?

options.text: Pre-agreed onboard procedures and trained crew autonomy within mission limits.
Waiting indefinitely for a reply even if the decision deadline passes.
Making an undocumented decision without checking safety rules.

questions.title: Message Prioritisation
questions.scenario: The communication link has limited bandwidth. Which information should be transmitted first during an emergency?

options.text: Crew safety, critical system status and information needed for support.
Routine entertainment files.
Large non-urgent science images before the emergency summary.

questions.title: Conflicting Instructions
questions.scenario: Two received messages appear to conflict. What should the crew do?

options.text: Verify message time and authority, then follow the approved command and safety process.
Choose the message with the shortest text.
Combine both instructions even if they are incompatible.

questions.title: Mission Timeline Change
questions.scenario: A repair takes longer than expected and affects a scheduled experiment. What should mission control do?

options.text: Re-plan around safety, task dependencies and available resources.
Keep the original timeline even when it is no longer feasible.
Skip required safety checks to recover the schedule.

questions.title: Crew Workload
questions.scenario: Several demanding tasks are assigned to the same crew member. What is the best planning response?

options.text: Balance workload, rest and task criticality, then assign work appropriately.
Assign every task to the same person.
Remove rest periods to finish the schedule.

questions.title: Emergency Drill
questions.scenario: Why should the crew practise emergency scenarios before they occur?

options.text: Practice improves readiness and can reveal gaps in procedures and equipment.
A drill guarantees that no emergency will occur.
Drills are useful only after an accident.

questions.title: Data-Storage Risk
questions.scenario: A rover is collecting unique scientific data but has limited storage and a weak communication link. What should it do?

options.text: Prioritise and validate key data, store it safely and transmit when the link allows.
Delete all data before checking it.
Transmit low-priority files first and ignore storage limits.

questions.title: Navigation Uncertainty
questions.scenario: A rover's estimated position becomes less certain near difficult terrain. What is the safest response?

options.text: Slow or pause, use available localisation methods and update the route.
Increase speed to spend less time in the area.
Ignore uncertainty and continue toward hazards.

questions.title: Mission Abort Criteria
questions.scenario: Why should a mission define conditions that require stopping or changing an activity?

options.text: Clear limits help the crew respond consistently when risk exceeds acceptable bounds.
Abort criteria prevent all equipment failures.
They allow the crew to ignore real-time conditions.

questions.title: Resupply Delay
questions.scenario: A planned cargo delivery is delayed. What is the best response?

options.text: Recalculate reserves, prioritise essentials and revise mission duration or activities.
Continue consumption as if the cargo had arrived.
Use emergency supplies for optional experiments.

questions.title: Radiation Exposure Records
questions.scenario: Why should astronaut radiation exposure be tracked over time?

options.text: To understand accumulated exposure and support informed health and mission decisions.
To convert every reading into a score only.
Because one reading predicts every future health outcome exactly.

questions.title: Using OSDR Research
questions.scenario: What is an appropriate way to use astronaut biological research data in an educational resource?

options.text: Explain relevant findings with context, limitations and clear source attribution.
Claim that one study proves every astronaut has the same outcome.
Present research data as a live radiation warning.

questions.title: Interpreting DONKI Events
questions.scenario: A space-weather database reports a coronal mass ejection. What additional information matters before creating a mission alert?

options.text: Event timing and available direction, speed and context, plus its relevance to the mission.
The event title alone.
A random danger score unrelated to the reported event.

questions.title: Food-System Resilience
questions.scenario: A greenhouse harvest is uncertain. Which strategy improves food-system resilience?

options.text: Combine crop planning, stored food, water and energy budgets, and contingency supplies.
Depend on one crop and discard stored food.
Assume plants always produce the expected harvest.

questions.title: Water-Recovery Efficiency
questions.scenario: A recycling system becomes less efficient. What should the crew monitor?

options.text: Input and recovered volumes, losses, system condition and water quality.
Only the colour of the storage tank.
The number of science experiments completed.

questions.title: Crew Exercise and Health
questions.scenario: Exercise equipment uses power and crew time. Why might exercise still be important?

options.text: Crew health is a mission requirement, so exercise must be planned alongside other needs.
Exercise should always use all available power.
Exercise removes the need for medical monitoring.

questions.title: Selecting Science Priorities
questions.scenario: Several experiments compete for limited power and crew time. How should they be prioritised?

options.text: Compare scientific value, resource demand, risk, timing and mission objectives.
Choose the experiment with the brightest display.
Run every experiment simultaneously regardless of limits.

questions.title: Reporting Uncertain Data
questions.scenario: A scientific measurement has a large uncertainty range. How should it be reported?

options.text: Show the value with units, uncertainty, method and limitations.
Report only the most exciting possible value.
Remove uncertainty to make the result look precise.

questions.title: Water Quality
questions.scenario: A sample of extracted ice has been melted for possible use by the crew. What must happen before consumption?

options.text: Process and test it to meet mission water-quality requirements.
Assume clear water is automatically safe to drink.
Use it without checking for contaminants.

questions.title: Learning from a Mission Failure
questions.scenario: A mission analysis shows the habitat ran out of power. What is the most useful next step?

options.text: Review decisions and resource trends, identify causes and revise the plan.
Hide the result and repeat the same decisions.
Assume the analysis is wrong without examining the evidence.

questions.title: Solar Event During EVA
questions.scenario: A solar particle event warning arrives while an astronaut is outside the habitat. What should the team prioritise?

options.text: Follow the EVA contingency plan and return the astronaut to appropriate protection as safely as possible.
Continue the task to avoid losing schedule time.
Disable radiation monitoring to reduce distractions.

questions.title: Power Failure and Oxygen Demand
questions.scenario: An electrical fault threatens both oxygen generation and research equipment. What should the controller do?

options.text: Allocate available power to essential life support and use backup procedures.
Keep research running at full power first.
Split power equally even if oxygen production becomes inadequate.

questions.title: Rapid Habitat Depressurisation
questions.scenario: Habitat pressure is falling faster than the crew can locate the leak. What is the best immediate strategy?

options.text: Protect the crew, use emergency procedures and isolate sections as directed.
Continue normal operations until the source is found.
Open additional compartments to search faster.

questions.title: Water and Crop Crisis
questions.scenario: A leak reduces water available for both the crew and crops. What is the best planning response?

options.text: Protect crew requirements, quantify reserves and adjust crop operations to the available water budget.
Give all water to crops because food is important.
Continue normal use and wait for the tank to empty.

questions.title: Rover Rescue Versus Crew Safety
questions.scenario: A stranded rover contains valuable samples, but rescue would consume a large energy reserve. What should guide the decision?

options.text: Compare rescue risk and resource cost against crew safety and mission-critical reserves.
Risk life-support reserves to recover every sample.
Redirect essential habitat power to the rescue without analysis.

questions.title: Multiple Critical Alarms
questions.scenario: Oxygen, temperature and communication alarms occur together. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Use the emergency priority framework, stabilise crew-critical systems and delegate tasks.
Handle the easiest alarm first regardless of consequence.
Silence all alarms and wait for Earth.

questions.title: Solar Array Damage Near Nightfall
questions.scenario: A damaged array needs repair, but darkness is approaching. What should the team consider?

options.text: Remaining daylight, battery reserve, repair risk and essential power demand before scheduling work.
Start the repair without checking the battery.
Wait until the batteries are empty.

questions.title: Unverified Radiation Reading
questions.scenario: A sensor produces an unusually high value that conflicts with other instruments. What should the crew do?

options.text: Treat it cautiously, verify instruments and follow radiation safety procedures while resolving uncertainty.
Delete the reading immediately.
Assume the lowest reading is always correct.

questions.title: Final Science Opportunity
questions.scenario: A rare experiment could provide major scientific value but uses energy needed for the coming night. What is the best decision process?

options.text: Check forecasts, life-support reserves and mission thresholds before deciding whether surplus energy is available.
Run it because rare opportunities must never be missed.
Disable the night-time power reserve.

questions.title: Thirty-Day Mission Assessment
questions.scenario: The outpost completes 30 days. Which measures best assess mission performance?

options.text: Evaluate crew safety, resource stability, system reliability and scientific objectives together.
Count only the number of experiments completed.
Count only the amount of power consumed.
